content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations regarding the use of uterotonics for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). These recommendations are based on updated evidence and aim to guide clinical practices and policies to reduce maternal morbidity and mortality associated with PPH. 1. Definition and Global Impact of PPH: Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours after childbirth. It affects approximately 5% of women globally and is responsible for nearly one-quarter of all maternal deaths, particularly in low-income countries where it is the leading cause of maternal mortality. 5. Global Maternal Health Goals: Efforts to prevent and manage PPH are critical to achieving the global target of reducing maternal mortality to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. Addressing PPH also helps reduce inequities in maternal and perinatal health worldwide. 6. Target Audience for Recommendations: These recommendations are intended for healthcare professionals involved in developing national and local guidelines, as well as those providing care during labor and childbirth, including midwives, nurses, general practitioners, obstetricians, and maternal health program managers. They are also relevant to policymakers and training institutions. 7. Guideline Development Process: The recommendations were developed using standardized WHO procedures, including identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination and implementation. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach for quantitative evidence and the GRADE-CERQual (Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research) approach for qualitative evidence. 8. Evidence-to-Decision Framework: The GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework was used to guide the formulation of recommendations. This framework considers intervention effects, values, resource use, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The recommendations were finalized during two Guideline Development Group (GDG) meetings in 2018. 9. Categories of Recommendations: Recommended: The intervention should be implemented. Not Recommended: The intervention should not be implemented. Context-Specific Recommendation: The intervention is applicable only under specific conditions, settings, or populations. Research-Context Recommendation: The intervention may be implemented as part of rigorous research to address uncertainties about its effectiveness, acceptability, and feasibility. 10. Implementation and Future Updates: WHO emphasizes the importance of correctly understanding and applying the recommendations in practice. Additional remarks and details are provided for context-specific recommendations. A systematic process will be employed to identify and address evidence gaps following implementation. If new evidence emerges, the recommendations will be updated accordingly. 11. Acknowledgments: WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations involved in updating these recommendations, including members of the Guideline Development Group, Evidence Synthesis Group, and External Review Group. The work was funded by USAID and the UNDP–UNFPA–UNICEF–WHO–World Bank Special Programme of Research in Human Reproduction (HRP). The funding bodies did not influence the content of the recommendations. 12. Summary of Recommendations: The updated recommendations on uterotonics for PPH prevention include four main recommendations and six sub-recommendations. These are based on assessments of the GRADE EtD criteria and are categorized to ensure clarity and applicability in various contexts. Derivative products, such as policy briefs, will be developed to facilitate the application of these recommendations at different levels of care. This document serves as a comprehensive guide for healthcare professionals and policymakers to implement evidence-based practices for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage, ultimately contributing to improved maternal health outcomes globally.
